prompt: Why did lessons 1 and 2 get away with reading `data/raw/clicks` from a local path?

choices.text: The master serves the file to the workers
choices.why: The master hands out cores and never touches data.

choices.text: Every executor was on the one machine that had the file
choices.why: Right. On a real cluster each worker would look on its own disk and find nothing.

choices.text: Spark copies a local file to every worker before the first task starts, so each finds its own copy
choices.why: It does not; each executor opens the path where it runs.

choices.text: Compressed files are readable from any machine
choices.why: Compression changes the size, not where the file is.

prompt: Match each way of storing a lake to what it is.
hint: One lives on the machines that compute; one is a service elsewhere.

pairs.right: Files spread over the disks of the cluster’s own machines
A separate service reached over the network

right_distractors: A copy of the data in the driver’s memory

prompt: What does the namenode store?
hint: It answers 'where is this file?' without touching a disk.

choices.text: The data of small files, and the metadata of large ones
choices.why: Size makes no difference; the namenode never stores file contents.

choices.text: The log of every job that read a file
choices.why: That is not HDFS's business at all.

choices.text: One copy of every block, for safety
choices.why: Datanodes hold all the copies; the namenode holds none.

choices.text: Metadata only
choices.why: Yes: the tree, the blocks of each file and where each copy is. No data.

prompt: Order the steps of reading a file from HDFS.
hint: The namenode is asked first and never carries the data.
items: The client asks the namenode which blocks make up the file
The namenode answers with the datanodes that hold each block
The client reads each block straight from a datanode

prompt: How many 128 MB blocks does a 1 GB (1,024 MB) file take in HDFS?
When a client writes a block, how do its three copies get made?
hint: The client sends the block once.

choices.text: Through a pipeline: datanode to datanode
choices.why: Right. The first passes it to the second as it arrives, and the second to the third.

choices.text: One copy is written now and two at night
choices.why: The write succeeds when all three hold the block.

choices.text: The client sends it three times, once to each datanode
choices.why: That would triple the client's traffic; the pipeline avoids it.

choices.text: The namenode copies it after the write
choices.why: The namenode never carries data.

prompt: Why is HDFS a poor disk to run a transactional database on?
hint: What can you not do to a file once written?

choices.text: Its blocks are too small for database pages
choices.why: They are huge, 128 MB; size is not the problem.

choices.text: A namenode refuses files that are open for long
choices.why: No such rule; the obstacle is in-place change.

choices.text: Files cannot be edited in place
choices.why: Right. A database rewrites pages all the time; HDFS only creates, appends and deletes.

choices.text: It keeps only one copy of each block, which is too risky for a database
choices.why: It keeps three.

prompt: Why does the setup put only Hadoop's `bin` on the path, and not its `sbin`?

choices.text: Hadoop has no `sbin` directory in the 3.5.0 release, only `bin` and `etc`
choices.why: It has one, with `start-all.sh` in it.

choices.text: `sbin` holds programs that only the root user is allowed to run on Ubuntu, so it stays off the path
choices.why: Hadoop's `sbin` scripts run as any user.

choices.text: To save memory
choices.why: The path costs no memory.

choices.text: Both projects ship a `start-all.sh`, and the second would quietly win
choices.why: Yes. A name clash on the path picks one silently.

prompt: Why does the lab run four datanodes rather than three, with replication of three?
hint: After losing one, where would a third copy go?

choices.text: To make writes four times faster
choices.why: All four share one disk here; the reason is the failure exercise.

choices.text: So that after losing one, three remain to hold three copies
choices.why: Right. With three datanodes, a lost one leaves nowhere for the third copy.

choices.text: One datanode per Spark worker, plus one more that the namenode needs for its own metadata
choices.why: The namenode needs no datanode of its own.

choices.text: HDFS needs an even number of datanodes so that every block has a partner on the opposite side
choices.why: No such rule.

prompt: Ana runs `sh hdfs.sh setup` a second time and starts everything. A datanode log says `Incompatible clusterIDs`. What happened?
hint: What does formatting give the filesystem?

choices.text: Two datanodes were given the same port
choices.why: That fails as an address already in use.

choices.text: The namenode ran out of memory
choices.why: Nothing here is large enough for that.

choices.text: The new format gave the namenode a new identity the datanodes do not recognise
choices.why: Right. Remove `~/hdfs`, then set up and start again.

choices.text: Java 17 is too new for Hadoop
choices.why: The first setup ran on the same Java.

prompt: The year's file is 1,291,239,322 bytes and a block is 134,217,728. How many blocks does it take?
hint: Round up: the last block holds what is left.

prompt: Ten blocks at replication three: how many block copies are on the datanodes' disks?
What is the small `.meta` file beside each block file for?
hint: It is checked on every read.

choices.text: The list of the other datanodes holding copies
choices.why: That is metadata, and the namenode keeps it.

choices.text: The block's checksums
choices.why: Yes. A damaged block is noticed and read from another copy.

choices.text: The name of the file the block belongs to
choices.why: Datanodes do not know file names; the namenode does.

choices.text: A compressed copy of the block
choices.why: It is tiny; it holds checksums.

prompt: Why does HDFS put a block's second and third copies on a different rack from the first?
hint: What is the commonest way to lose several machines at once?

choices.text: So a rack losing power cannot take every copy
choices.why: Right. Machines in one rack share power and a switch.

choices.text: A rack can hold only one copy of any block, by a rule HDFS enforces whatever the replication
choices.why: The second and third share a rack.

choices.text: To spread the namenode's memory
choices.why: Placement does not change what the namenode stores.

choices.text: Reads from another rack are faster, because the switch in each rack is shared by fewer machines
choices.why: They are usually slower; the rule is about surviving.

prompt: Why does the namenode wait before copying a silent datanode's blocks elsewhere?
hint: What does copying cost, and what else could silence mean?

choices.text: It cannot know which blocks were there
choices.why: It knows exactly, from the block reports.

choices.text: Silence is no proof of death, and copying costs the whole cluster
choices.why: Right. Copying terabytes for a datanode that comes back a minute later would be waste.

choices.text: A client has to ask for the repair
choices.why: Nobody asked; the namenode did it on its own.

choices.text: The blocks must first be read back from the dead datanode
choices.why: The copies come from the survivors, not the dead one.

prompt: When datanode 2 died, the file was short of copies but could still be read throughout. Why?
hint: How many copies did each affected block still have?

choices.text: Each affected block still had two
choices.why: Right. Reading needs one.

choices.text: The namenode served the missing blocks itself
choices.why: The namenode holds no data.

choices.text: Spark had cached the file in memory
choices.why: No job was running; HDFS alone kept it readable.

choices.text: Datanode 2 held no blocks of that file
choices.why: It held seven of the ten, which is why seven were short.

prompt: If all three machines holding a block fail together, `fsck` reports the file as ___.
Seven blocks of 128 MB were copied to restore replication. About how many MB moved?
The same petabyte in files of 1 MB instead of 1 GB. What grows, and where?
hint: The data did not get bigger.

choices.text: Nothing that matters
choices.why: It decides whether the namenode copes.

choices.text: The disk space on the datanodes, by about a thousand times
choices.why: Disk use stays about the same; the bytes are the same bytes.

choices.text: The number of copies of each block
choices.why: Replication stays three.

choices.text: Objects in the namenode's memory
choices.why: Right. About 2 billion objects instead of 9 million.

prompt: Why will Spark be slower reading the 365 daily files than the one file of ten blocks, for the same events?

choices.text: 365 tiny tasks each pay the fixed cost per task
choices.why: Right. Ten tasks of a full block spend their time reading.

choices.text: Daily files are stored with fewer copies
choices.why: Replication is three for both.

choices.text: gzip cannot be read by Spark
choices.why: Lesson 1 read them fine.

choices.text: The namenode refuses more than 100 files per job
choices.why: No such limit.

prompt: A job that reads many small files and rewrites them as a few large ones is called ___.
Stage 1 of `hdfs_count.py` ran ten tasks, all `NODE_LOCAL`. What does that mean?

choices.text: The tasks ran inside the namenode, which is the process that knows where every block is kept
choices.why: Tasks run in executors.

choices.text: Each read its block from a disk in its own machine
choices.why: Right. No block crossed the network.

choices.text: Each read its data from the executor's memory, where an earlier stage of the same job had left it
choices.why: That is `PROCESS_LOCAL`, lesson 9.

choices.text: The data was copied to the driver first
choices.why: The driver never received the blocks.

prompt: Order Spark's locality levels from best to worst.
Without `dfs.datanode.hostname`, every reading task ran at `ANY` on one machine. Why?
hint: How does Spark decide two things are on the same machine?

choices.text: The file was too large to read locally
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with locality.

choices.text: The executors were busy, so Spark gave up waiting
choices.why: Even an idle executor would not have matched `localhost`.

choices.text: HDFS forbids local reads by default
choices.why: Nothing forbade them; Spark did not recognise the host.

choices.text: Spark matches names, and `localhost` was not `127.0.0.1`
choices.why: Right. Same machine, two names, and locality silently off.

prompt: How do you rename an object in an object store?

choices.text: By editing its key in place with a metadata request, leaving the bytes where they are
choices.why: Nothing about an object is edited in place.

choices.text: With one rename request, which the store carries out without moving a byte of the object
choices.why: The S3 API has none.

choices.text: Copy it under the new key, then delete the old one
choices.why: Right. Two requests, and the copy moves every byte.

choices.text: By moving its directory
choices.why: There are no directories, only keys.

prompt: `s3_demo.py` listed 31 'folders'. What were they really?

choices.text: Empty objects whose names end in a slash
choices.why: Some tools create those, but this program did not.

choices.text: Buckets
choices.why: There was one bucket, `pontofinal-lake`.

choices.text: Directories created by `create_bucket`
choices.why: A bucket is created empty; there are no directories in it.

choices.text: Key prefixes, grouped up to the next slash
choices.why: Right. No folder object exists.

prompt: Moving 50,000 objects one by one, as `s3_demo.py` moved 31, takes how many requests?
A job moved from HDFS to an object store, unchanged, writes 10,000 files. What goes wrong at the end?

choices.text: Every move becomes a copy, slowly, and readers meanwhile see half the result
choices.why: Right. Slow and not atomic, and no error says so.

choices.text: It fails, because object stores refuse temporary directories
choices.why: It runs; the trouble is quieter than a failure.

choices.text: The files are written with one copy instead of three
choices.why: The provider keeps its own copies.

choices.text: Nothing, since the path is the only change
choices.why: The path is the only change in the code, not in the behaviour.

prompt: How does a table format make a write appear all at once on an object store?

choices.text: It renames the files faster than Hadoop does
choices.why: It does not rename at all.

choices.text: It locks the bucket while writing
choices.why: Object stores have no bucket locks.

choices.text: It writes all the data into a single object
choices.why: Data stays in many files; only the commit is one.

choices.text: One small commit file lists the table's files
choices.why: Right. Writing one file is atomic anywhere.

prompt: Which column makes a good partition for the clicks?
hint: Few values, and what queries filter on.

choices.text: `day`
choices.why: Right. 365 values, and almost every question names a period.

choices.text: `visitor_id`
choices.why: Two million values: two million directories of tiny files.

choices.text: `event_id`
choices.why: Unique per row, the worst choice there is.

choices.text: `ts`, to the second
choices.why: Over thirty million values in a year.

prompt: Match each layer of a lake to what it holds.

pairs.right: The data as it arrived, never edited
The same data, cleaned and typed

prompt: A team shuts its cluster down every night to save money. Where should its data live, and why?
hint: Where does HDFS keep the bytes?

choices.text: An object store: HDFS lives on the cluster's own disks
choices.why: Right. Shut the machines and HDFS is gone; the object store stays.

choices.text: Either; replication keeps it safe when the cluster is off
choices.why: Replication is across the cluster's machines, which are off.

choices.text: HDFS, because it is faster to read
choices.why: Speed does not help data that vanished with the machines.

choices.text: The driver's disk
choices.why: One machine's disk is the problem this lesson started from.

pairs.right: One change in the namenode’s memory
